description: Inspirados en la grandeza del Imperio Inca y su profunda conexión con la cosmovisión andina, somos un equipo multidisciplinario que une ciencia, tecnología e innovación para transformar desafíos de nuestra realidad en soluciones de impacto global.
summary: We developed Yachiraq, a mobile-first decision-support tool that helps smallholder farmers in Chiara (Ayacucho, Peru, 3,000–4,300 m) choose a 3-year crop rotation for each field that protects their soil and water. It combines NASA Earth observations (SRTM/NASADEM, NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP and MODIS NDVI) with soil data and Andean crop traits to compare the farmer's current rotation with a soil-building and a water-saving alternative, explaining the evidence, risks and uncertainty behind each one. It also sends frost and heavy-rain alerts by WhatsApp. This matters because Andean families often repeat the same crops on steep fields, which exhausts the soil and builds up pests, while the climate is becoming less predictable and there are very few weather stations in the highlands. Our own satellite analysis shows it: between 15 October and 14 November 2026, Chiara received 20% less rain than normal and its soil was 22% drier, and a field at 3,820 m faces about 142 frost nights a year. Yachiraq turns global satellite data into clear, field-level advice that supports, rather than replaces, farmer knowledge.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Yachiraq is a decision-support tool for crop rotation planning in the Andean highlands. Specifically:

- It maps each farmer's field on a real 3D terrain model and measures its area, elevation, slope and altitude zone (Quechua, Suni or Puna).

- It compares three 3-year crop rotations side by side: the farmer's current rotation, a soil-building rotation based on legumes and cover crops, and a water-saving, market-oriented rotation.

- It shows, month by month over 36 months, when the soil would be left bare during heavy rain and when a crop would flower during frost.

- It explains every recommendation: why it was suggested, the data behind it, its benefits, risks, information gaps and a confidence level.

- It sends frost and heavy-rain alerts by WhatsApp, with concrete actions such as covering seedlings with straw or clearing drainage ditches.

Yachiraq home screen: real 3D terrain of Chiara (SRTM/NASADEM) with the pilot area outlined. The app is available in Spanish and English.

How does it work?

User flow: farmers can explore Doña Rosa's example or map their own field, answer five questions, and get a field page with four tabs. The rotation comparison supports the decision, but the farmer decides.

1. Field mapping: the farmer locates the field with GPS or taps its corners on the 3D map. Elevation is sampled at up to 50 points inside the field (SRTM/NASADEM) and the slope is estimated with a least-squares plane fit.

2. Farmer input: five questions about current and previous crops, planting month, planned next crop, purpose (household or market), irrigation and livestock.

3. Data fusion to one value per field per month:

- NASA POWER climatology, adjusted to the field's elevation (0.65 °C per 100 m) and bias-corrected against a local reference. Without this correction, the coarse POWER grid cell over Chiara would report frost on almost every night of the year.

- Monthly frost nights estimated from the corrected minimum temperature.

- GPM IMERG rainfall over the last 30 days compared with the same period in the previous 20 years, and SMAP soil moisture anomaly, both computed in Google Earth Engine.

- MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI compared with the same date over the previous 3 years, via the ORNL DAAC web service.

- ISRIC SoilGrids organic carbon, texture and pH, and an Open-Meteo 7-day forecast at the field's exact elevation.

4. Simulation and scoring: each rotation is simulated for 36 months using planting windows and growing times for 12 Andean crops, then scored on seven criteria (soil fertility, erosion protection, water demand, frost tolerance, pest-cycle breaking, market value and forage). Erosion risk uses a USLE-style cover factor weighted by monthly rainfall and slope. The farmer picks up to two priorities, and the ranking updates instantly.

5. Alerts: a scheduled serverless function runs every day at 05:00 (Lima time) and sends a WhatsApp message when frost (0 °C or below) or heavy rain (15 mm/day or more) is forecast.

Field view: the farmer's field drawn on the 3D map, with a GPM IMERG and SMAP rainfall anomaly alert and concrete actions for the current potato crop.

Side-by-side comparison of three 3-year rotations, scored on seven criteria and weighted by the farmer's priorities. The soil-building rotation reduces bare-soil months from 21 to 18 and scores 69 vs. 41 for the current rotation. The map shows the field's planned crop sequence over time.

What benefits does it have?

Environmental: makes soil degradation visible and encourages rotations with legumes and ground cover, which reduce erosion on steep slopes and restore soil fertility.

Social: gives farming families clear, local advice in plain Spanish, plus early warnings for frost and heavy rain on their phones, in a region with very few weather stations.

Economic: helps protect harvests from frost, lowers the risk of pest build-up from repeated crops, and highlights crops with market value, such as quinoa and tarwi.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, we want to validate the model with farmers and extension agents in Chiara, comparing its recommendations with their experience and with INIA crop data. In the long term, we want to connect the official SENAMHI forecast, compute the rainfall and soil anomalies automatically every day, add market prices and Quechua audio, and adapt the tool to other Andean districts. NASA data is global, so scaling mainly requires adapting the crop list, altitude zones and local climate reference.

What makes it creative?

Instead of a black-box model, we built transparent rules that agronomists and farmers can read and correct, because there is no local yield data to train a reliable machine-learning model. The app also shows the limits of remote sensing: it corrects satellite bias against a local reference and displays a confidence level for every recommendation. It is designed for rural users: plain language, crop illustrations, a highly legible typeface for bright sunlight, text-to-speech, Spanish and English, and no account required.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Programming languages: JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3

Frontend and visualization: vanilla JavaScript single-page app (no build step, light enough for low-end phones), MapLibre GL JS 3D terrain, SVG charts and illustrations

Backend and automation: Netlify Functions (Node.js) and Netlify Scheduled Functions for the daily alert

Data processing: Google Earth Engine (JavaScript API) for GPM IMERG and SMAP anomalies

Data APIs: NASA POWER, ORNL DAAC MODIS Web Service, ISRIC SoilGrids, Open-Meteo

Maps and imagery: AWS Terrain Tiles, Esri World Imagery

Messaging: Green-API (WhatsApp) and Twilio (SMS fallback)

Hosting and version control: Netlify, Git and GitHub

Security: phone-number allowlist, rate limiting, and API keys stored only as environment variables

What factors did your team consider?

Connectivity (the app falls back to reference values when an API does not respond), scientific honesty (crop rules are general FAO and INIA references that must be validated locally, and the app says so), privacy (data stays on the farmer's phone), and scope (Yachiraq is a pilot for the Chiara district and does not give recommendations outside it).

Links

Live app: https://yachiraq.netlify.app/?lang=en

Video demo and slides: https://canva.link/dis8htujbrtifa9

Source code: https://github.com/Juanjo166/Yachiraq

Use of AI

Claude (Anthropic): code generation and review for the web app, serverless functions and Google Earth Engine script; English translation of the interface; and help writing documentation.

The decision model inside the app does not use AI: it is a transparent, rule-based model.
